title: Town Reconstructed / Savoy Mississippian / College Established
text:
Town Reconstructed

Reconstruction began at once. The first two blocks, running north and south on Water street, and as many directions now. As the town progressed, and the west block of bricks on the north side of the street were torn away, the buildings were built. One by one the old wood buildings were torn away, and the bricks took their places. Two or three of the old buildings to be torn down are the Drugstore building owned by the late W. L. Teague. After Mr. Teague's death P. O. Teague took over the cleaning. It stood north of the H. H. Arterberry store.

The Gooseberry has served Savoy and the surrounding community in the drug and grocery trade for almost half a century. He established the business in 1892, in what was almost an unpopulated place. After the establishment of the Savoy Tribune, later known as the Savoy Star, H. H. Arterberry was connected with it for a time. After his withdrawal, the newspaper was operated until his son Max was through school, and was made a partner. It now operates under the name Arterberry and Son. Mr. Arterberry was born and raised in Savoy. He has education in the Savoy College.

The Savoy Tribune, later known as the Savoy Star, was first published about 1890, and by 1902, when T. E. Arterberry and L. H. King established the Savoy Star. Mr. King operated the Savoy Star only a short time, then Mr. Arterberry bought out King. Arterberry continued the work together for 23 years when he was claimed by his calling. He left the family alone until her marriage to J. B. May, who is her assistant. The family is dry now and has a Washington hand press of which there is one of the best in the state here today. Besides the local news, advertising, and editorials, Mrs. May has tried to save local history, aided by many who are compiling scrap-books.

Had Flour Mill

In the spring of 1900 there was a flour mill here, located north of the old school building. In 1902 a new elevator was built, known as the Womack Milling Co. It was a place of milling for several years before it was torn down. Until recent years there has been a cotton gin here at one time and at night in the fall. They now have a modern gin up and have not been replaced.

Savoy Mississippian

It has been recalled that in 1884 a man known as "Parson Smith" was minister; there were several before him and quite a few between him and the late Postmaster W. P. Carter. Mr. Carter served a number of years the first appointment, then H. M. Arnon, now of Denton, served eight or nine years. Mr. Carter was reappointed and will serve until December 16, 1941. Claude Strickland recently was appointed postmaster here.

College Established

The Savoy College was established in 1880 when Prof. J. L. Halsell, served as a local school for Savoy and surrounding communities. Through the years Prof. Halsell decided to enlarge the school into a college and applied to the state for a charter, which was granted Jan. 22, 1880, to H. R. Halsell and others; also C. E. Paxton and J. L. German, with the name "Savoy Female College" or "Female College." It is spoken of today as the Savoy College or the Halsell College. The school, much like the school of today, consisted of a grammar school, high school and college all in one system.

The highest degree to be conferred was an A. B. degree. The school did not put much stress on athletics. There were literary and debating societies were more popular. The school had two literary societies, the Platahian, for the older boys, and the Philomathians for the younger ones. The students were made "Keepers of Governmental Laws." Under this system each student was required to write an essay each week. A lady of Spanish descent taught French and Spanish. Among those taught in the school during its 14 years were H. R. Harshaw, R. R. Halsell, Lewis Holman, Watt Pritchard, R. A. Gay and Mr. Henshaw.

College Is Destroyed

The College burned in the fall of 1913, and was never rebuilt. Many of the records, books, and other valuable records were destroyed. Miss Lou Arterberry, an ex-student who had a photograph of part of the school bell that went through the fire and is using it for a door stop.

Prof. Halsell died in Durant, Okla., and is buried in Durant.

The first ex-student reunion was held in August 1937, when the new rock Halsell Memorial Building was finished. The reunion is to be on the same date.

The next school building for Savoy was a two-story wood building, located north of the present building of the school. It was built about 1914. Mr. Hendricks was in charge of the school work for the next five or six years, but an old record that was apparently in the 1920s shows there were four teachers then. The one on the blackboard, W. E. McMahon and Miss Marsha Buford, now Mrs. J. B. May. The routes of Savoy and Mahurin were combined. Owens going to Mahurin and he replaced Miller, Dodson was sent to Bonham, replaced it, this time one story. The school here is provided with modern equipment. There is a modern rock gym on the west, where the F. F. A. class meets, and the bot[?] 13 tennis room is located. There are 13 telephone directors, two recreation directors, six employed in the lunch room. The Randolph Grove school has been consolidated with the Savoy school, the New Warren school, transferred to the Mahurin was also transferred.

Savoy Mississippian

Col. William Louis Marshall Savoy, founder of the town of Savoy, was born Aug. 2, 1817, in Mississippi, died Sept. 1, 1887, in Goshee, Johnson County, Texas.

He came to Texas at an early age, settling first near home, Texas, near the present city of Sherman. The place is known today as the Savoy Prairie.

During the civil war, he enlisted in the Confederate army, but refused active duty while in training and never saw active service. The next few years were spent in travel. He crossed the Atlantic twice and the Pacific three times. It is believed, according to Mrs. Louise Travis, that he was doing secret service work for the government at this time.

Col. Savoy often remarked that he had every kind of contagious disease, except yellow fever, while on an adventure trip in South America. He had secured a large tract of valuable land, but when he fell ill with a tropical disease, without he left very hurriedly, never going back to claim it.

Joined Gold Rush

In 1849 he joined the crowd in the gold rush to California, making a fast trip across country. The gold laden hills he dug with picks and shovels the gold nuggets with his own hands were sent back to Savoy. The gold was carried back to Savoy. It is a story often recalled by Mrs. Travis that her father was robbed twice by bands of Indians, who fought with tomahawks and arrows, once while taking cotton to a San Antonio market from Goshee, Texas.

About 1854, he was making a trip through West Texas by train. An Indian attack or possible one, in front of Col. Savoy, turned and said, "You are the bravest man I've met there," Col. Savoy, remembering the attack replied "Well, my friend you are mistaken."

In 1874 Col. Savoy was married to Mrs. Julia E. Davis, in Savoy. The couple went to Denison to live. When returning from a trip, they were met by the hometown band and escorted to their home. Several churches were located and the Methodist Church building was given to the members of Church of Christ as well as all the other denominations.

The Christian Church was established in the summer of 1838, with a minister by the name of Graves of Sherman. Mr. Graves served as pastor until the fall of [text continues but is cut off]
